terms: Acrylic paint
Fast-drying water-based paint developed in mid-twentieth century, used by David Hockney in his California pool paintings.
Alla prima
Wet-into-wet painting method completed in a single session, favoured by Impressionists such as Monet.
Glazing
Application of thin translucent layers over a dried underlayer, deepening colour and luminosity in oil painting.
Impasto
Thick application of paint creating visible texture and brushmarks, used dramatically by Van Gogh and Frank Auerbach.
Oil paint
Pigments suspended in drying oil, allowing slow blending and glazing, used by Old Masters and contemporaries like Lucian Freud.
Underpainting
Monochrome or limited-palette layer establishing tonal structure before full colour is applied.

Acrylic paint

Alla prima
Wet-into-wet painting method completed in a single session, favoured by Impressionists such as Monet.
Glazing

Impasto

Oil paint

Underpainting
Monochrome or limited-palette layer establishing tonal structure before full colour is applied.
Brand identity
Coherent visual system including logo, typography and colour palette communicating an organisation's character.
CMYK
Four-colour subtractive printing process using cyan, magenta, yellow and black, standard for full-colour printed work.
Grid system
Underlying structure organising layout into columns and rows, popularised by Swiss design in the 1950s.
Hierarchy
Visual ordering of information by size, weight, colour and placement so the viewer reads the most important content first.
Negative space
Unoccupied area around and between elements in a design, used actively by Saul Bass in his film posters.
Vector graphic
Image defined by mathematical paths rather than pixels, allowing scaling without loss of quality, used in logos.
Aperture
Adjustable opening in the lens controlling light intake and depth of field, measured in f-stops such as f/1.8 or f/16.
Composition
Arrangement of visual elements within the frame, using devices such as the rule of thirds, leading lines and framing.
Decisive moment
Henri Cartier-Bresson's concept of the perfect split-second capturing the essence of an event, central to documentary photography.
Depth of field
Range of distance appearing acceptably sharp in an image, controlled by aperture, focal length and subject distance.
ISO
Sensitivity of the sensor or film to light, with higher values enabling low-light shooting but adding grain or noise.
Shutter speed
Duration the sensor or film is exposed to light, determining motion blur or freezing, measured in fractions of a second.
Batik
Indonesian wax-resist dyeing technique creating patterns by applying molten wax to areas that resist dye.
Embroidery
Decorative needlework on fabric, ranging from traditional samplers to contemporary art by Tracey Emin.
Felting
Process of matting wool fibres together using moisture, heat and pressure, producing dense non-woven fabric.
Pattern repeat
Unit of design that tiles across a fabric, with options including straight, half-drop and brick repeats.
Screen printing
Stencil-based printing technique using mesh screens, used commercially for textiles and by artists from Warhol onwards.
Warp and weft
Vertical (warp) and horizontal (weft) threads interlaced in weaving, the foundation of woven textile structures.
Architectural model
Three-dimensional representation of a building at reduced scale, used to communicate spatial relationships and design intent.
Ceramics
Practice making objects from clay fired at high temperature, encompassing functional pottery and sculptural ceramics.
Interior design
Practice shaping the inside of buildings through spatial planning, surfaces, lighting and furniture.
Jewellery design
Discipline producing wearable adornment, ranging from precious metalwork to contemporary art pieces by makers like Wendy Ramshaw.
Product design
Discipline developing functional manufactured objects, balancing form, ergonomics, materials and user experience.
Set design
Creation of physical environments for theatre, film and television, supporting narrative and character.

unit-a2-1-personal-and-critical-investig.d: Unit A2 1: Personal and Critical Investigation
terms: Annotation
Written reflection alongside visual work, analysing intentions, processes, influences and outcomes for assessment.
Contextual analysis
Examination of a work's historical, social and cultural conditions of production, beyond purely formal qualities.
Critical study
Investigation of artists, movements and works that informs and contextualises a student's own practical development.
Personal investigation
Extended A-Level component in which students develop a self-directed enquiry supported by a written element of around 1000-3000 words.
Primary research
First-hand investigation through gallery visits, life drawing or photography, generating original source material.
Secondary research
Investigation drawn from existing sources such as books, online archives and reproductions, supporting primary work.
Development
The visible progression of an idea through experiments, studies and revisions on the way to a final piece.
Evaluation
Reviewing the strengths and weaknesses of an outcome against your intentions to justify final decisions.
Personal response
An outcome expressing your own interpretation of the theme rather than a copy of source material.
Refinement
Improving a chosen idea by adjusting composition, scale, colour or technique in response to review.
Resolved outcome
A finished artwork that realises your stated intentions, showing refinement of ideas, media and technique.
Theme
The central idea or starting point that unifies a body of work, sustained from investigation through to the final outcome.
Annotation
Short written notes explaining what you tried, what you learned and what you plan to do next.
Experimentation
Trying out a range of media, techniques and processes to discover possibilities before committing to ideas.
Media exploration
Testing materials such as paint, ink, print, collage or digital processes to learn their qualities and limits.
Portfolio
A curated collection of experimental work showing breadth of investigation and the journey of your ideas.
Primary sources
First-hand material you record yourself — observational drawings, your own photographs, objects and places.
Risk-taking
Deliberately trying unfamiliar approaches and learning from unexpected results rather than playing safe.
